parts.title: Assigned Desks Are Quietly Coming Back to Some Offices
parts.part1:
One office question is quietly coming back:

“Where is my desk?”

After the pandemic, many companies adopted hot-desking. Workers were not given one permanent desk. Instead, they chose an open desk when they arrived.

The system allowed companies to share workstations instead of giving one desk to every employee.

But some employers are now moving in the other direction. They are bringing back assigned desks or using hot-desking less often.

This change has been reported at some companies. It was also discussed at an office conference, with comments from office and real estate leaders.

For employees, the complaint can be simple.
parts.part2:
An open desk may change every day. Workers may sit beside people they do not know. One survey says employees can value a workspace that is predictable and consistent. They may also see hot-desking as less attractive than working from home.

These points help explain employee dissatisfaction. But they do not prove that one single factor caused it.

Hot-desking is still important in many workplaces. One report, citing workplace data, said the share of workers using hot-desking had doubled from before the pandemic, reaching 20%.

At the same time, this is not a full return to the old office.

The move back to assigned desks is limited to some companies and departments. Many businesses are still using shared desks and flexible space.

So the office story is now split.

Some teams want flexibility. Others want a clear place to sit.
parts.point_one_heading: A desk can feel like more than furniture
parts.point_one_body: One report found a link between assigned seating and two feelings: belonging and focus. Among workers with assigned desks, 87% reported a sense of belonging, compared with 74% in unassigned settings. The focus figures were 80% and 67%. The data shows a link, not proof of cause.
parts.point_two_heading: The wider office is still sharing
parts.point_two_body: A 2024 survey points in the other direction. The share of companies with one desk per employee or fewer fell from 56% in 2023 to 40% in 2024. Respondents expected it to reach about one-third by 2026. Desk sharing remains the wider pattern.
parts.in_one_line: Hot-desking is not disappearing, but in some offices, the personal desk is quietly finding its way back into the plan.

parts.title: 🪑 The Quiet Return of the Assigned Desk
parts.part1:
After the pandemic, many offices changed how people sit at work.

Instead of giving each person a desk, they introduced hot-desking. A worker comes in, finds an empty desk, and uses it for the day. No personal desk is waiting.

Now, some offices are changing again. Reports show some companies bringing back assigned desks for certain workers or teams. In this system, a person or team has a regular place.
parts.part2:
The change is quiet. It is not a return to fixed desks across every office. In some workplaces, it is a response to complaints about shared seating and the daily search for a place to work.

So the office story is not simply, “Shared desks are gone.” Some companies are adding fixed seats, while companies overall still have fewer desks for their workers.

The result is a mixed picture. One team may choose any free desk each morning. Another may have its own regular area.

The question is now simple:

Is maximum flexibility always the best way to work?
parts.point_one_heading: A desk can feel like a home base
parts.point_one_body: Why are some workers pushing back? One report says hot-desking may feel less attractive than home, and sitting beside unfamiliar colleagues can be uncomfortable. Workers may also value a predictable, consistent place. One survey found stronger feelings of belonging with assigned desks: 87% versus 74%. This is a link, not proof that the desk caused the difference.
parts.point_two_heading: Flexibility is still the larger trend
parts.point_two_body: Still, this is not a full return to one desk for every person. One report found that the share of companies with at least one desk per employee fell from 56% in 2023 to 40% in 2024. Respondents expected about one-third by 2026. Sharing remains common, even as some teams choose assigned seats.
parts.in_one_line: Assigned desks are making a quiet comeback as some workplaces respond to the wish for a stable place to work. But shared seating is still the wider trend, so the future may be a mix of both systems.
